Machines mock paper

How to use this: this is a new paper, not a past paper. Sit it under exam conditions 2 days before the exam: 120 minutes, timer on, your printed notes and reference sheet only, calculator. Do not open the marking guide until time is up. Then mark yourself strictly with the guide and use the score table at the end to plan your last 24 hours.

Instructions

  • Total duration: 120 minutes.
  • This examination is open book. Hardcopy printed and handwritten materials are allowed. No electronic devices apart from a calculator without remote communication.
  • Attempt ALL FOUR questions. All questions carry equal marks (20 each, 80 in total). Part marks are given in brackets.
  • Show your working. Method marks are given for correct equivalent circuits and correct substitutions, even when the final number is wrong.
  • Phasors are rms. Unless stated otherwise, three-phase voltages are line-to-line and three-phase powers are totals.
  • Answers should be expressed clearly and written legibly. These aspects of presentation will be taken into account in assessment.

Time budget: 1.5 minutes per mark, so 30 minutes per question. Keep the last 5 minutes to check angles, signs and units.

Question 1 [20 marks]

AC and DC Power Circuit Analysis

1a) DC power and efficiency [5 marks]

A DC motor is supplied from an ideal 48 V DC source through a cable. The total resistance of the cable (go and return conductors together) is 0.12 Ω. The motor draws 40 A and delivers a mechanical output power of 1.5 kW at 1200 rpm.

  1. Find the voltage at the motor terminals and the power lost in the cable. [2 marks]

  2. Find the electrical input power to the motor, the motor efficiency and the motor output torque. [3 marks]

1b) Delta-connected load [6 marks]

A balanced three-phase load is connected in delta to a 415 V, 50 Hz, three-phase supply. Each phase of the load is a 24 Ω resistor in series with an inductive reactance of 18 Ω.

  1. Find the phase current (magnitude and phase, with the phase voltage as reference), the line current magnitude and the power factor of the load. [3 marks]

  2. Find the total real power and the total reactive power absorbed by the load. [2 marks]

  3. The same three impedances are reconnected in star to the same supply. Find the new total real power. [1 mark]

1c) Power-factor correction [9 marks]

A small factory is supplied at 415 V, 50 Hz, three-phase. Its load consists of the delta-connected load from part 1b (connected in delta, as in parts (i) and (ii)) in parallel with a three-phase induction motor. The motor drives a mechanical load of 18 kW with an efficiency of 90 % and a power factor of 0.75 lagging.

  1. Find the total real power, the total reactive power, the power factor and the line current drawn from the supply. [3 marks]

  2. A bank of three capacitors is to be added in parallel with the factory to raise the supply power factor to 0.95 lagging. Find the total reactive power that the capacitor bank must absorb, and the new line current. [3 marks]

  3. The three capacitors are connected in delta. Find the required capacitance of each capacitor. [2 marks]

  4. How much reactive power would the capacitor bank need to absorb to give 0.95 leading instead? Give one reason why this is not done. [1 mark]

Question 2 [20 marks]

Magnetic Circuits and Transformers

2a) Electromagnetics [7 marks]

A magnetic core is made from two identical U-shaped halves placed with their ends facing each other, so that the flux crosses two airgaps in series, each of length 0.4 mm. The core has a rectangular cross-section of 4 cm × 3 cm everywhere, a mean magnetic path length in the iron of 36 cm (total for both halves), and a relative permeability of 2500. A coil of 200 turns is wound on one of the halves. Neglect fringing.

  1. Calculate the reluctance of the iron, the reluctance of one airgap and the total reluctance, and hence the inductance of the coil. [3 marks]

  2. Find the DC coil current needed to produce a flux density of 1.2 T in the core, and the total energy stored in the two airgaps at this flux density. [2 marks]

  3. At 1.2 T, find the total force pulling the two halves of the core together. [2 marks]

2b) Transformer parameters [5 marks]

The following tests are performed on a single-phase 3300 V : 240 V, 20 kVA, 50 Hz transformer.

  • Open-circuit test, performed on the low-voltage (240 V) side with the HV side open: 240 V, 2.6 A, 135 W.
  • Short-circuit test, performed on the high-voltage (3300 V) side with the LV side shorted: 145 V, 6.06 A, 290 W.

Find all the simplified equivalent circuit parameters (, , and ), referred to the high-voltage (primary) side.

2c) Transformer performance [8 marks]

The transformer of part 2b supplies its rated kVA at rated secondary voltage (240 V) to a load with a power factor of 0.8 leading. Use the simplified equivalent circuit with the magnetising branch at the primary terminals, and take the referred secondary voltage as the phase reference.

  1. Find the referred secondary current and the primary voltage required, both in polar form. [3 marks]

  2. Find the voltage regulation in percent. Explain in one sentence why its sign is what it is. [2 marks]

  3. Find the efficiency at this load. [1 mark]

  4. Find the load (in kVA) at which this transformer has maximum efficiency, and the value of that maximum efficiency at 0.8 power factor. Assume rated voltage. [2 marks]

Question 3 [20 marks]

AC and Induction Machines

3a) AC machines [6 marks]

A three-phase AC machine has a nameplate showing 60 Hz and a rated speed of 1164 rpm.

  1. How many poles does it have? Is it a synchronous machine or an induction machine? Briefly explain why. [2 marks]

  2. Find the rated slip and the frequency of the rotor currents at rated speed. [1 mark]

  3. At rated speed, what is the ideal (that is, maximum possible) efficiency of the machine? [1 mark]

  4. The machine is operating at one-half of rated torque. Assuming a linear torque versus speed curve, find the operating speed in rpm and the output power as a percentage of rated output power. [2 marks]

3b) Induction machine parameters [5 marks]

The following tests are performed on a 400 V, 50 Hz, three-phase induction motor whose stator is delta-connected. All voltages and currents below are line values as measured at the motor terminals, and all powers are three-phase totals.

  • Stator resistance: 2.8 Ω per phase winding.
  • No-load test: input voltage 400 V, input current 4.2 A, input power 320 W.
  • Blocked-rotor test: input voltage 92 V, input current 10 A, input power 620 W.

Find the simplified equivalent circuit parameters per phase of the delta: , (the total leakage reactance ), and .

3c) Induction machine calculation [9 marks]

A 415 V, 50 Hz, six-pole, three-phase, star-connected squirrel-cage induction motor has the following equivalent circuit parameters per phase (referred to the stator where appropriate):

  • stator resistance = 0.6 Ω, rotor resistance = 0.45 Ω
  • stator leakage reactance = 1.2 Ω, rotor leakage reactance = 1.2 Ω
  • magnetising reactance = 40 Ω, core-loss resistance = 300 Ω

Use the simplified equivalent circuit (magnetising branch across the input terminals). Friction and windage can be neglected. The motor runs at rated voltage at 970 rpm.

  1. Find the synchronous speed, the slip and the effective rotor resistance . [2 marks]

  2. Find the referred rotor current and the input phase current (magnitude and phase, with the phase voltage as reference), and the input power factor. [3 marks]

  3. Find the input power, the airgap power, the output torque and the efficiency. [3 marks]

  4. Find the slip and the speed in rpm at which maximum torque occurs. [1 mark]

Question 4 [20 marks]

Per-Unit and Synchronous Machines

4a) Synchronous machine tests [5 marks]

A 60 MVA, 13.8 kV, 50 Hz, three-phase, star-connected synchronous generator gives the following test results at a field current of 180 A:

  • open-circuit line voltage: 9.2 kV
  • short-circuit current: 1.25 kA

The stator resistance is 0.05 Ω per phase. Use rated values as the per-unit base.

  1. Find the base impedance and the base current. [1 mark]

  2. Find the synchronous reactance in ohms and in per-unit. [3 marks]

  3. What field current gives rated voltage on open circuit? Assume the open-circuit characteristic is linear. [1 mark]

4b) Generator at leading power factor [7 marks]

The generator of part 4a is connected to a large grid at rated terminal voltage. It delivers 45 MW at a power factor of 0.85 leading. Neglect the stator resistance and saturation.

  1. Find the terminal voltage and the stator current phasors in per-unit, with the terminal voltage as reference. Find also the stator current in kA. [2 marks]

  2. Find the excitation voltage in per-unit, the rotor angle, and the field current. [3 marks]

  3. With the field current held at this value, the operator tries to raise the real power output to 60 MW. Find the theoretical maximum power, in MW, that the generator can deliver without losing synchronism, and say whether 60 MW is possible. If it is not, find the minimum field current that would make 60 MW theoretically possible. [2 marks]

4c) Short-answer questions [8 marks]

Answer the following questions using words only (that is, without any sketches, drawings or equations).

  1. A synchronous generator is connected to a large power grid. Explain what is meant by over-excited and under-excited operation, and explain how the field current and the mechanical input power each affect the real and reactive power delivered. [3 marks]

  2. The speed of an induction motor can be reduced either by adding resistance to the rotor circuit of a wound-rotor machine, or by using an inverter to reduce both the supply voltage and the frequency. Explain why the first method is inefficient and why the second is not. [3 marks]

  3. Explain why the per-unit system is useful when analysing a power system that contains transformers. [2 marks]

END OF QUESTIONS

4c) Short-answer questions [8 marks]: model points and marks

You do not need every point for full marks. Roughly one mark per well-explained point.

(i) Over- and under-excitation [3 marks]

  • The field current sets the excitation voltage. When a generator is connected to a large grid, the grid fixes the terminal voltage and the frequency.
  • Over-excited: the field current is higher than needed for the terminal voltage. The generator delivers reactive power to the grid and runs at a lagging pf, like a capacitor seen from the grid.
  • Under-excited: the field current is lower. The generator absorbs reactive power from the grid and runs at a leading pf. This weakens the magnetic coupling, so the maximum power before losing synchronism is lower (as in 4b(iii)).
  • Mechanical input power (prime mover) controls real power: more input torque advances the rotor angle, and more real power is delivered. The speed stays at synchronous speed.
  • Field current controls reactive power: at a fixed real power, changing the field current mainly changes the reactive power and the pf.

(ii) Rotor resistance vs V/f speed control [3 marks]

  • In an induction machine, the airgap power splits into rotor copper loss (the slip fraction) and mechanical power (the rest). So the ideal efficiency is one minus the slip, the ratio of rotor speed to synchronous speed.
  • Extra rotor resistance lowers the speed by increasing the slip, while the synchronous speed stays the same. At large slip, a large part of the airgap power is wasted as heat in the rotor circuit and the external resistance. At half speed, at least half the airgap power is lost.
  • An inverter that lowers the frequency lowers the synchronous speed itself. The torque–speed curve slides to lower speed with the same shape, so the motor still runs at a small slip and the rotor losses stay small. Efficiency stays high.
  • The voltage is reduced in proportion to the frequency to keep the flux constant. This avoids saturation and keeps the maximum torque available.

(iii) Per-unit system [2 marks]

  • Quantities are expressed as fractions of chosen base values, so the normal operating values are near 1 and abnormal values are easy to see.
  • If the base voltages on each side of a transformer are chosen in the ratio of its turns, the per-unit impedance is the same from both sides, and an ideal transformer disappears from the per-unit circuit. You do not have to refer impedances across each transformer.
  • Machine and transformer parameters fall in narrow per-unit ranges regardless of size, so values are easy to check and compare. The single-phase and three-phase per-unit values are the same, which removes the factors of 3 and root 3.

Common mistakes:

  • Using equations or symbols. The question says words only.
  • In (i), mixing up which knob controls what. Field current is for reactive power. Prime mover is for real power.
  • In (ii), saying the first method is inefficient “because of the resistor” without saying why: the slip is large and rotor loss is the slip fraction of the airgap power.

Score interpretation

Mark each part strictly, then add up each question out of 20. Use the table below to decide what to do in your final 24 hours. Do not try to re-learn everything. Fix the one or two weakest areas, and then do the “everyone” list.

Your result What it means What to do
64–80 (80 %+) Exam-ready. Light review only. Re-do one part you lost marks on, then read through your reference sheet and the 4c model points. Sleep.
48–63 (60–79 %) Solid. One or two topics are leaking marks. Use the per-question rows below for any question under 15/20. Spend about 60 minutes on each weak question, not more.
32–47 (40–59 %) Method is there but errors cost a lot. Look at why you lost marks. If it was mostly signs, and star/delta, re-do the traps sections of M2, M7 and M10. If it was not knowing where to start, work through the playbooks (section 2) of the packs for your two lowest questions.
